blocks.text: Earnest and Practical Effort of Close Application

inline.s: After I left home, I went about visiting and seeking instruction. At that time Master Bianrong’s teaching was greatly flourishing, and I

went to the capital to pay my respects to him, kneeling as I advanced and making my request again and again. The master said: “Keep your own lot; do not pursue fame or run after profit, do not seek to rise by clinging to others.
Only make clear the distinctions of cause and effect, and be single-minded in reciting the Buddha.

” I received his instruction and withdrew. My fellow travelers burst out laughing, thinking that any of them could have said these words: having come from a thousand li away, we imagined there would be something extremely marvelous, yet in the end it was not worth half a copper. I said: “This is precisely where his goodness lies. We thirsted and longed for him and came so far. Yet he did not speak of the mysterious or discourse on the subtle, looking down upon
He simply and plainly, in a matter-of-fact way, set before us the close, practical, and real effort he had himself realized, earnestly admonishing us with it.
This is why it is his goodness.” To this day I have honestly kept and observed it, and have not let it go.

[Master Bianrong] an eminent monk of the Ming dynasty; his deeds are recorded in the Sequel to the Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks. [The close, practical, and real effort he had himself realized] this sentence fully shows that Master Lianchi had a uniquely discerning eye, going after none of the grand but empty “high doctrines” that are mere talk on paper, and so he benefited for the rest of his life.
Make clear cause and effect, and be single-minded in reciting the Buddha,”
these eight gold-glinting great characters are in truth the motto of every Buddha-recitation practitioner.

[Cause and effect clear] to deeply know “such a cause, such a fruit,” and therefore to be on guard over one thought, one word, one deed of one’s own, so that the good fruit is abundant. Hence the sutra says: “The bodhisattva fears the cause; the ordinary being fears the fruit.” Beings create evil out of greed and anger because they do not know cause and effect, do not believe in cause and effect, or else profess belief with the lips while not truly believing it. Once the evil fruit appears, they are panic-stricken and fearful, at a loss what to do. [Single-minded in reciting the Buddha] single-minded means mind following mind without interruption, with no other thought mingling in. (See
Single-minded recitation of the Buddha is supremely excellent:
Single-minded recitation of the Buddha brings the three studies of discipline, concentration, and wisdom to full completion.
Master Lianchi, in his Pure Land Collected Sayings of Yunqi, says:
Discipline means guarding against wrongdoing. If one is
, all evils dare not enter — that is discipline. Concentration means removing distraction. If one is
, the mind does not fasten on other objects
(the mind does not bind itself to other things)

— that is concentration. Wisdom means clear illumination. If one contemplates the Buddha-sound so that each word is clear and distinct, and also contemplates that both the one who recites and what is recited are unobtainable, that is wisdom. To recite the Buddha in this way is discipline, concentration, and wisdom.”

(Translation: discipline means guarding against wrongdoing; if one can be single-minded in reciting the Buddha, all evils dare not enter, and this is discipline. Concentration means removing distraction; if one is single-minded in reciting the Buddha, the mind does not bind itself to other things, and this is concentration. Wisdom means clear illumination; if one contemplates the Buddha-sound so each word is clear and distinct, and also contemplates that the one who recites and what is recited are both unobtainable, this is wisdom. Reciting the Buddha in this way is discipline, concentration, and wisdom.)
Single-minded recitation of the Buddha brings the six perfections and the myriad practices all to completeness.
Master Lianchi, in his Commentary on the Amitabha Sutra, says:
, the myriad conditions naturally cast themselves aside — that is the perfection of giving;
, all evils naturally cease — that is the perfection of moral precepts;
, the mind naturally becomes gentle — that is the perfection of patience;
, one never retreats — that is the perfection of diligence;
, other thoughts do not arise — that is the perfection of meditation; single-minded in reciting the Buddha, right mindfulness is clear — that is the perfection of wisdom. Pushing it to the utmost,
it does not depart from the single mind
(it does not depart from single-minded recitation of the Buddha)
, and the myriad practices are all complete.”

(Translation: now if one is single-minded in reciting the Buddha, the myriad conditions naturally cast themselves aside, and this is the perfection of giving; if one is single-minded in reciting the Buddha, all evils naturally cease, and this is the perfection of moral precepts; if one is single-minded in reciting the Buddha, the mind naturally becomes gentle, and this is the perfection of patience; if one is single-minded in reciting the Buddha, one never retreats, and this is the perfection of diligence; if one is single-minded in reciting the Buddha, other thoughts do not arise, and this is the perfection of meditation; if one is single-minded in reciting the Buddha, right mindfulness is clear, and this is the perfection of wisdom. Extending it to all practices without exception, single-minded recitation of the Buddha brings the myriad practices to completeness.)

[Myriad practices] all manner of practice. The Essay on the Bodhi Mind says: “After passing through three great asamkhyeya kalpas, cultivating the six perfections and the myriad practices, all fully complete, one then realizes Buddhahood.”
[The bodhisattva fears the cause, the ordinary being fears the fruit

] Master Yinguang says: “The sutra says: ‘The bodhisattva fears the cause; the ordinary being fears the fruit.’ The bodhisattva, fearing the evil fruit, cuts off the evil cause in advance. Thus his karmic hindrances are destroyed, his merit is fulfilled, and he goes on until Buddhahood is attained and only then stops. The ordinary being always creates evil causes, yet wishes to escape the evil fruit — like one who runs from his own shadow in the daylight, laboring in vain.” (from Collected Writings of Master Yinguang, Primarily Edited, the Letter to Wei Jinzhou)
Question: Since it is “such a cause, such a fruit,” why is it that cutting off evil and practicing good can transform one’s destiny?

Answer: Karma is the cause, and its fruit is the karmic fruit. For the karmic fruit to appear, there must be the appropriate conditions. In our past lives we created much evil karma and also much good karma. Cutting off evil and practicing good not only cuts off the evil karma and creates good karma, planting more good causes, but also forms the conditions that bring the good fruit (the karma of good) to appear and removes the conditions that would bring the evil fruit (the karma of evil) to appear. In this way calamity departs and fortune arrives, and destiny is transformed.

blocks.text: Human Life Is at the Breath’s End

inline.s: The essential gate of entering the Way takes faith as first. Even evil, if not believed in, is not brought to completion — how much less good? Consider the thieves of the world: when they are exposed, the authorities do not fail to punish them with the severest penalties. And when
afterward, once released, they still do not repent. Why is this? Because they believe in this path, and for the cost of
a single coin of capital, they gain profit beyond all reckoning. And so, though they endure bitter suffering, they never retreat into regret.

The essential gate of entering the Way takes faith as first. If evil, not being believed in, is not brought to completion, how much less good? Consider the thieves of the world: when exposed, the authorities do not fail to punish them with the severest penalties. But when they are released after serving their term, they still do not repent. Why? Because they believe firmly in this path, and for no more than the cost of a single coin of capital they obtain profit beyond counting. And so, though they endure bitter suffering, they never retreat into regret.

People today, in reciting the Buddha, are unwilling ever again to be truly earnest in applying effort, simply because they have never deeply reflected and sincerely believed. Put aside not believing in the Pure Land — take even this one saying of the World-Honored One:
“Human life is at the breath’s end,”

this sentence, in terms of its meaning, is not hard to explain. You have seen it with your own eyes and heard it with your own ears, passing through many examples of it. Yet now to have you believe this sentence — you are already
unable to do so. If you could truly believe this sentence, then the Dharma gate of Buddha-recitation would not require me to spend my strength exhorting you a thousand and ten thousand times
for you would of yourself flow like water into a deep ravine
, which ten thousand oxen could not drag back.

People today, in reciting the Buddha, even when admonished again and again, are unwilling to be truly earnest in applying effort — only because they have never deeply reflected and sincerely believed. Put aside not believing in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss; take even this one saying of the World-Honored One, “Human life is at the breath’s end” — in principle it is not hard to understand and explain. You have seen it with your own eyes and heard it with your own ears; there have already been many actual instances of “human life at the breath’s end.” Now, to have you believe this saying, “human life is at the breath’s end,” you have long been unable to do so. If you could truly believe this saying, then the Dharma gate of Buddha-recitation would not require me to exhaust my strength and exhort you a thousand and ten thousand times; you would of yourselves flow downward like the water of the mountains into a ravine, which ten thousand oxen could not drag back.

[Human life is at the breath’s end] In the Sutra of Forty-two Sections, the Buddha asked a monk: “How far does human life lie between?” He answered: “In a few days.” The Buddha said: “You have not yet understood the Way.” He asked another monk: “How far does human life lie between?” He answered: “Between a meal.” The Buddha said: “You have not yet understood the Way.” He asked yet another monk: “How far does human life lie between?” He answered: “At the breath.” The Buddha praised him: “Excellent! You have understood the Way!” (The original reads:

“The Buddha asked a monk: ‘How far does human life lie between?’ He answered: ‘Within a few days.’ The Buddha said: ‘My son, you have not yet understood the Way.’ He asked again of a monk: ‘How far does human life lie between?’ He answered: ‘Within a meal.’ The Buddha said: ‘My son, you have not yet understood the Way.’ He asked again of a monk: ‘How far does human life lie between?’ He answered: ‘At the breath.’ The Buddha said: ‘Excellent! My son, you have understood the Way!’”

) [At the breath] — within the space of a breath life may be cut off; this is what is meant by “the out-breath being not guaranteed to be followed by the in-breath.” The Buddha here makes it clear: human life is impermanent, the out-breath being not guaranteed to return as an in-breath; so the student of the Way must be vigilant and diligent, striving to complete the career of the Way before death overtakes him.
Take only the other day, when we saw off a deceased monk — you saw this example, and should have been saddened and distressed
, and earnestly admonished one another, saying: “All! You and I are today escorting one monk and tomorrow escorting another. Before we know it, our turn comes.
Then regret will be too late

we must make haste to recite the Buddha, not letting the moment slip by” — that would be well. Yet I see you say among yourselves that it is a pity, and say to others that it is a pity; but when it comes to the valuation and auction in the hall, you talk and laugh as freely as ever. You simply do not believe that human life is at the breath’s end!

Take only the other day, when we saw off a deceased monk — you saw with your own eyes the arrival of death, and you should have been solemn and grave, and earnestly admonished one another, saying: “All! You and I are without end today escorting one monk and tomorrow escorting another. Before we know it, our turn comes. At this point regret would be too late; we must now make haste to recite the Buddha, not letting the moment slip by, so as to accomplish the career of the Way before death arrives — that would be good.” I see you say to yourselves that his career of the Way was not accomplished and his death is a pity, and say to others that his career of the Way was not accomplished and his death is a pity. But when it comes to the valuation and auction of his belongings in the hall, you talk and laugh as freely as ever. You simply do not believe that human life is at the breath’s end!

[Seeing off] the sending off of a deceased monk is called “seeing off” at a monastery. [Then regret will be too late] to repent only at the point of death that one was earlier not diligent enough and did not accomplish the career of the Way is too late — this is truly a pity beyond measure! [We must make haste to recite the Buddha, not letting the moment slip by] to accomplish the career of the Way before death arrives. [A pity] to grieve that the deceased monk passed away without his career of the Way being accomplished. [Valuation and auction] the belongings of the deceased monk are distributed to the monks present; first the value is set, called “valuing the things,” and then they are auctioned before the assembly, called “auctioning the things.”

The Rhapsody on the Epang Palace says: “The men of Qin had no leisure to grieve for themselves, and so the men of later ages grieved for them; and when the men of later ages grieve for them without taking them as a warning, they make the men of still later ages grieve once more for them.” (Translation: the men of Qin had no leisure to grieve over their own destruction, and had to let the men of later ages grieve for them; and if the men of later ages only grieve without taking it as a warning, then their own destruction would in turn be grieved over by the men of still later ages.) — To grieve but not to take warning: a sigh shared by ancient and modern alike!
[Not taking warning] not drawing the lesson.
The Universal Worthy (Samantabhadra) Bodhisattva’s Admonitory Verse says:
This day has passed / And life has diminished with it; / Like a fish in diminishing water, / What joy is there in
this? / All of you: / Be diligent and zealous, / As though your head were on fire! / But be mindful of impermanence
(but be mindful of the coming of death)
, / And in no way be lax and indolent
(and in no way give yourself to idle pleasure)

[Fish in diminishing water] a fish in a pond whose water is daily drying up. [Be diligent and zealous, as though your head were on fire] the great fire above your head is blazing, and death is drawing near with haste; reciting the Buddha, you should be diligent and unremitting, quickly and yearningly to extinguish this fire of death, so as to complete the

before death and confusion overtake you. [Impermanence] — that which has no permanent dwelling (all things of the world arising and ceasing, flowing and changing, not abiding even for an instant); it also refers to death, the spirit that seizes the soul. [In no way be lax and indolent] — do not on any account give yourself over to idle pleasure and waste your spirit and time. The Buddha said: “
Though one toils for a single life, in a brief space one is reborn in the Land of Immeasurable Life, with joy beyond measure.”
(From the Sutra of the Buddha’s Sermon on the Buddha of Immeasurable Life)

blocks.text: Gathering and Sinking, Again and Again

inline.s: I see beginners who, the moment they set a single word of the Buddha upon their minds, find that idle thoughts and false imaginings seem to boil and surge all the more, and thereupon say that the practice of Buddha-recitation cannot gather the mind. You do not know that this false thinking is the root and origin of your birth-and-death through countless kalpas — how can it be cut off all at once? And at the very moment when the ten thousand thoughts are flying about is precisely the time for doing the practice. Gathering and sinking, sinking and gathering, over and over; when after a long time the practice becomes fully mature, the false thoughts will naturally not arise. And as for your being able to notice that the false thoughts are heavy — you have this single word of the Buddha to thank
you have this single Buddha-name to thank
. If at the time you are not reciting the Buddha, false thoughts roll like waves and surge like the tide, not pausing for an instant — could you of yourself be aware of them?

I see beginners who, the moment they set a single word of the Buddha upon their minds, find that idle thoughts and false imaginings seem to boil and surge all the more, and thereupon say that the practice of Buddha-recitation cannot gather the mind. They do not know that this false thinking is the root and origin of your birth-and-death through countless kalpas — how can it be cut off at once? And at the very moment when the ten thousand thoughts are flying about is precisely the time for doing the practice. Gathering and sinking, sinking and gathering; practicing on in this way, after a long time the practice becomes fully mature, and the false thoughts naturally do not arise. And as for your being able to notice that the false thoughts are heavy — it is due to this single word of the Buddha. If at the time you were not reciting the Buddha, false thoughts would roll like waves and surge like the tide, not pausing for an instant — could you of yourself be aware of them?

[Gathering (xuan)] straightaway. [Gathering and sinking, sinking and gathering] — the moment one gathers the thought onto the Buddha-name, it immediately scatters (false thoughts arise); the moment the thought scatters, one immediately gathers it again onto the Buddha-name. “Gathering and sinking” describes the beginner’s recitation of the Buddha; the remedy for it is “sinking and gathering.” [If at the time you were not reciting the Buddha, false thoughts roll like waves and surge like the tide, not pausing for an instant — could you of yourself be aware of them?]
If at the time one is not reciting the Buddha, false thoughts roll like waves and surge like the tide, not pausing for an instant — could one of oneself be aware of them?

Beginners do not have the skill of becoming aware at the very rising of a thought, and often sink into false thinking without being able to notice it — let alone free themselves from it. This is creating the karma of transmigration. So one must on all account recite the Buddha more, in order to lessen the time spent in false thinking that creates the karma of transmigration, and to increase the time devoted to the Pure Land karma, while at the same time improving one’s skill in reciting the Buddha.
[Pure Land karma] the karmic cause of rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.

In reciting the Buddha there is silent holding, loud holding, and vajra holding. Yet the loud seems too laborious, and the silent easily turns drowsy. Only the continuous and close, the sound dwelling between the lips and the teeth, is called vajra holding. Nor may one fix upon it in a rigid way. If one feels it laborious, then it is fine to hold silently
or if one feels drowsy, then it is fine to hold aloud. Those who recite the Buddha today merely tap the wooden fish

and call out at random, and so gain no benefit. Each word must issue from the mouth and enter the ear, each sound awakening one’s own self-mind. It is like a man sunk in heavy sleep, and another calling: “So-and-so!” — whereupon he at once wakes. This is why reciting the Buddha is best able to gather the mind.

In reciting the Buddha there is silent holding, loud holding, and vajra holding. Yet the loud holding seems too laborious, and the silent holding easily turns drowsy. Only the continuous and close, the sound dwelling between the lips and the teeth, is vajra holding. Yet one cannot rigidly fix on any one of them. If one feels it laborious, then it is fine to hold silently; if one feels drowsy, then it is fine to hold aloud. Those who recite the Buddha today merely tap the wooden fish and call out at random, and so gain no benefit. Each word must issue from the mouth and enter the ear, each sound awakening one’s own self-mind. It is like a man sunk in heavy sleep, and another calling: “So-and-so!” — whereupon he wakes (a metaphor for the self-mind waking up from false thinking). This is why reciting the Buddha is best able to gather the mind and remove false thinking.
[Merely tap the wooden fish and call out at random, and so gain no benefit]
Master Hanshan’s Song of Wasted Leisure in his Dream Travels Collection says:
“With the mouth reciting Amitabha while the mind is scattered / Even to split the throat by calling is in vain.” (See
“The Essential Points of Chan and Pure Land”
People today will not recite the Buddha, simply because they make light of the West

not knowing that reborn in the West is an undertaking of great virtue and great fortune, of great wisdom and great understanding, of great sages and great worthies, turning Saha into the Pure Land — no small matter of ordinary conditions.

People today are unwilling to put forth bitter effort to recite the Buddha only because they regard rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss as too easy, not knowing that rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss is an undertaking that only those of great virtue and great fortune, of great wisdom and great understanding, of great sages and great worthies, can take upon themselves; and that to be reborn from this Saha world into the Land of Ultimate Bliss is not something to be accomplished through ordinary conditions.

[Merely make light of the West] only because one regards rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss as too easy. Though all know that “ten recitations at the point of death, if continuous, bring rebirth,” they take this continuity of ten recitations too lightly, thinking that they will be able to accomplish it at the point of death. On this, Master Daochuo instructs: however, the minds of all ordinary beings are like wild horses and their consciousness like apes, galloping over the six objects (forms, sounds, scents, tastes, tangibles, and ideas) — have they ever rested for a moment? So, each person must resolve on a single mind of faith, and beforehand train himself to single-minded concentration, thought following thought continuously,
so that through practice it becomes second nature

(through continual practice, make the mind’s single-mindedness, thought following thought continuously, become a second nature). Only then can the ten continuous recitations be accomplished at the point of death. Otherwise, when the knife-wind of death arrives and a hundred sufferings press down in scorching pain, if beforehand one has not achieved the single-mindedness of thought following thought continuously as a second nature, then at the point of death merely wishing to accomplish the “ten continuous recitations” — how could it be done? (For the original text and notes, see
) [Small and trivial] ordinary, negligible. For example: “no small matter.”

You look only at this city: in one day, one night, how many people die? Put aside rebirth in the West — even among those reborn in heaven, there is not one in a thousand. Among those who are self-conceited in their practice, they only manage not to lose the human body.

You look only at this city: in one day and one night, how many people die? Put aside rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss — even for rebirth among the heavens, there is not one in a thousand. And of those who are conceited and rely on their own strength in practice, they only manage not to lose the human body.
Therefore our World-Honored One, in his great compassion and great pity, pointed out this Dharma gate. His merit overpasses heaven and earth, his kindness surpasses father and mother
even to grinding our bones to powder and shattering our bodies, we could not repay it!

Therefore our World-Honored One, in his great compassion and great pity, pointed out this Pure Land Dharma gate. His merit overpasses heaven and earth, his kindness surpasses father and mother — even to grinding our bones to powder and shattering our bodies, we could not repay it!
[Merit overpasses heaven and earth] his merit surpasses heaven and earth. Qian-kun (qian kun): heaven and earth.
When I was young I did not yet know how to recite the Buddha. I saw an elderly neighbor woman

who each day recited the Buddha several thousand times. I asked, “Why do you do so?” She answered, “My late husband, when he was alive, recited the Buddha, and his passing was very good, so I recite like this. When my late husband passed away, he had no other illness, only a single farewell, and he left.” How can we who have left home fail to recite the Buddha?
how to recite the Buddha, and I saw an elderly
in the neighboring household who each day
recited the Buddha, and when he went he
too. When my late husband went
saying “Goodbye” and leaving. (This paragraph is a modern rendering of the passage above.)
